Fit a survival (hazard) model of leaving the service

fit_survival_model.Rd

Estimates how covariates such as gender or occupation change the chance of leaving the service in a given year, for people of the same tenure in the same year, separately for retiring and for leaving otherwise.

The effects are hazard ratios (see tidy.survival_model()): 0.8 for women means a woman is 20% less likely to leave in a given year than a comparable man.

Usage

fit_survival_model(panel, ...)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
fit_survival_model(
  panel,
  covariate_cols = attr(panel, "covariate_cols"),
  exit_types = c("retired", "other"),
  band_width = 1,
  period_effects = TRUE,
  make_tidy_output = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_dbi'
fit_survival_model(
  panel,
  covariate_cols = attr(panel, "covariate_cols"),
  exit_types = c("retired", "other"),
  band_width = 1,
  period_effects = TRUE,
  make_tidy_output = FALSE,
  ...
)

# Default S3 method
fit_survival_model(panel, ...)

Arguments

panel

A survival_panel from build_survival_panel(), in memory or in a database.

...

Passed to fixest::fepois(), e.g. nthreads, or notes = TRUE to see fixest's own notes (off by default). Not fml, data, offset, vcov, ssc, weights or cluster (see Details).

covariate_cols

Character vector. The covariates to model. Defaults to those the panel was built with; character(0) for tenure (and year) effects only.

  • A character column becomes categories, compared with its first value in alphabetical order. To compare with another, make it a factor with that level first.

  • A numeric column enters linearly, per unit: for pay, that is per unit of currency. Cut it into bands first (e.g. pay quintiles): the hazard ratios are easier to read, and people stay added up into few groups (a column with a value per person makes a group per person).

exit_types

Any of "retired" and "other" (both by default). An exit type no one had is left out, with a warning.

band_width

Number. The width in years of the tenure bands within which the chance of leaving is taken as constant. Default 1.

period_effects

Logical. If TRUE (the default), each calendar year gets its own level of exits, absorbing shocks that hit everyone in a year.

make_tidy_output

Logical. If TRUE, return the hazard ratio table from tidy.survival_model() instead of the model. Default FALSE.

Value

A survival_model, for tidy.survival_model() and predict.survival_model(); fixest's own functions (summary(), coef(), fixest::fixef(), fixest::etable()) work on it too. With make_tidy_output = TRUE, the hazard ratio table instead.

Details

Model. A piecewise-constant proportional hazards model, fitted as a Poisson regression of exits (fixest::fepois()) with a log(exposure) offset and fixed effects for tenure band (the baseline hazard) and, with period_effects, calendar year. One model per exit type gives cause-specific hazards. The result is fixest's output (a fixest_multi, or a fixest for one exit type) with class survival_model added.

Groups, not people. The panel is first added up into groups of people with the same tenure band, snapshot date and covariate values (in the database, for a database panel). Exit counts and years at risk are sufficient statistics for a Poisson model, so the estimates and standard errors equal those on the person-level panel; fixest's number of observations is the number of groups.

Missing values. A person-interval with no tenure or a missing covariate cannot be modelled: it is left out, with a warning that counts them.

Standard errors are the model's own (vcov = "iid"), with no small-sample adjustment, which would depend on the number of groups. As fml, data, offset, vcov and ssc are set here, and weights or cluster would be wrong on grouped data, ... cannot pass them.

Tenure and year. Within a person, tenure and year rise together, so with both sets of fixed effects the hire cohort is implied: the model assumes the shape of the hazard over tenure is the same for every cohort.

See also

build_survival_panel() for the panel, tidy.survival_model() for the hazard ratios, predict.survival_model() for predictions.

Examples

library(data.table)
contracts <- as.data.table(bra_hrmis_contract)
personnel <- as.data.table(bra_hrmis_personnel)
tenure <- compute_tenure_panel(contracts)
personnel <- merge(personnel, tenure, by = c("personnel_id", "ref_date"), all.x = TRUE)

panel <- build_survival_panel(
  personnel, contracts,
  tenure_col = "tenure_years", salary_col = "gross_salary_lcu",
  status_col = "employment_status", covariate_cols = "gender"
)
fit <- fit_survival_model(panel, band_width = 5)
#> Warning: 54 person-intervals have a missing value in `tenure_years` or `gender` and are left out of the model.
summary(fit)
#>                               x.1              x.2
#> Dependent Var.:      exit_retired       exit_other
#>                                                   
#> genderMASCULINO -0.3311* (0.1298) -0.1133 (0.1127)
#> Fixed-Effects:  ----------------- ----------------
#> .band                         Yes              Yes
#> .year                         Yes              Yes
#> _______________ _________________ ________________
#> S.E. type                     IID              IID
#> Observations                  137              164
#> Squared Cor.              0.79424          0.82637
#> Pseudo R2                 0.53249          0.62053
#> BIC                        421.75           487.41
#> ---
#> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# hazard ratios
broom::tidy(fit)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 10
#>   exit_type term   covariate level estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low
#>   <chr>     <chr>  <chr>     <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 retired   gende… gender    MASC…    0.718     0.130     -2.55  0.0107    0.557
#> 2 other     gende… gender    MASC…    0.893     0.113     -1.01  0.315     0.716
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: conf.high <dbl>
